title: PM Analytics Interview Cheat Sheet
description: 30+ concepts covering metrics, visualizations, statistical tools, product analysis tools, and rapid revision

metrics.name: DAU
metrics.definition: Count of unique users who perform at least one session or action in a single day.
metrics.when_to_use: When measuring daily product health, engagement velocity, or impact of a daily-habit feature.
metrics.example_answer: Instagram's DAU is a north star — if a push notification change drops DAU by 3% next day, we roll back immediately.
common_mistakes: Confusing sessions with users
Not defining what 'active' means (login vs meaningful action)

metrics.name: WAU
metrics.definition: Count of unique users who are active within any rolling 7-day window.
metrics.when_to_use: For products with weekly natural cadence — work tools, news, B2B SaaS.
metrics.example_answer: Notion's WAU/MAU ratio of 0.7 tells us most monthly users actually return weekly — strong retention signal.
common_mistakes: Using calendar weeks instead of rolling 7 days — creates artificial Monday spikes

metrics.name: MAU
metrics.definition: Count of unique users active within a rolling 30-day window.
metrics.when_to_use: For reporting product scale, investor metrics, or low-frequency products (travel, tax).
metrics.example_answer: Our MAU grew 15% QoQ, but DAU/MAU dropped from 0.4 to 0.3 — users are signing up but not forming habits.
common_mistakes: Treating MAU growth as a success signal without checking DAU/MAU ratio — hides engagement hollowness

metrics.name: Retention
metrics.definition: Percentage of users who return and perform a meaningful action after a defined interval post-signup.
metrics.when_to_use: Whenever product health, long-term value, or feature stickiness is in question.
metrics.example_answer: D30 retention is 22%. Industry benchmark for social apps is 20–25%. Our D7 is strong at 55% but D30 drops sharply — the product hooks users early but loses them in week 2.
common_mistakes: Using login as retained instead of core action
Not segmenting by acquisition channel
Ignoring resurrection rate

metrics.name: Churn
metrics.definition: Percentage of users or revenue lost within a defined period, typically monthly or annually.
metrics.when_to_use: When diagnosing subscription health, predicting revenue impact, or evaluating product-market fit degradation.
metrics.example_answer: Monthly churn is 5%. At this rate, we lose ~46% of users annually. We need to cut churn to 2% to hit ARR targets — that means addressing core pain points in week 2.
common_mistakes: Confusing user churn with revenue churn
Not measuring involuntary churn (payment failures) separately

metrics.name: Conversion Rate
metrics.definition: Percentage of users who complete a desired action out of those who had the opportunity.
metrics.when_to_use: When analyzing funnels, testing checkout flows, evaluating onboarding, or pricing page changes.
metrics.example_answer: Our free-to-paid conversion is 3.2%. SaaS benchmark is 2–5%. The bottleneck is step 3 of checkout — 60% of drop-offs happen there. An A/B test on payment form reduced friction and lifted it to 4.1%.
common_mistakes: Reporting aggregate CVR without segmenting by traffic source or device
Not controlling for seasonality in tests

metrics.name: Engagement Rate
metrics.definition: Proportion of users performing a specific meaningful action (like, share, comment, click) out of total users exposed.
metrics.when_to_use: When evaluating content quality, feature adoption, or campaign effectiveness.
metrics.example_answer: Our feed engagement rate dropped from 18% to 12% after the algorithm change. Breaking it down: likes down 10%, shares down 40% — shares are disproportionately impacted, suggesting the new ranking deprioritizes viral content.
common_mistakes: Treating all engagement equally (a like ≠ a share ≠ a comment)
Not weighting by event value

metrics.name: Activation Rate
metrics.definition: Percentage of new signups who reach the 'aha moment' — the first action that predicts long-term retention.
metrics.when_to_use: When diagnosing onboarding problems or evaluating the impact of an onboarding redesign.
metrics.example_answer: Only 34% of signups complete profile setup — our defined activation event. Data shows activated users have 3x higher D30 retention. Fixing onboarding is our highest-leverage bet this quarter.
common_mistakes: Defining activation as signup (trivially easy) instead of the first meaningful value moment
Setting it too hard and missing real activation

metrics.name: LTV
metrics.definition: Total predicted revenue a customer generates over their entire relationship with the product.
metrics.when_to_use: When setting CAC targets, justifying growth spend, evaluating customer segments, or pricing decisions.
metrics.example_answer: LTV = ARPU / churn rate = $40/month ÷ 5% = $800. With CAC at $120, LTV/CAC = 6.7x — healthy. But enterprise segment LTV is $8,000 vs SMB at $400. We should reallocate sales resources.
common_mistakes: Using simple average LTV across segments
Ignoring time value of money
Not separating gross margin LTV from revenue LTV

metrics.name: CAC
metrics.definition: Total cost spent on sales and marketing divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period.
metrics.when_to_use: When evaluating channel efficiency, growth sustainability, fundraising projections, or payback period.
metrics.example_answer: Our blended CAC is $120. Paid CAC is $320 vs organic $40. We're spending heavily on paid but it has 2x higher churn — organic customers are 3x more valuable. Shift budget to SEO and referral.
common_mistakes: Using blended CAC only and missing channel-level efficiency differences
Including existing customer upsell spend in CAC

visualizations.name: Line Chart
visualizations.definition: Plots a continuous metric over time with data points connected by lines.
visualizations.when_to_use: Any time you're tracking a metric over time — trend, growth, seasonality, or anomaly detection.
visualizations.example_answer: I'd plot DAU on a 90-day line chart segmented by platform. The drop becomes visible on Day 14 — it aligns with the iOS update rollout. Line comparison shows Android DAU flat, isolating the iOS bug.
common_mistakes: Not annotating events (launches, outages) on the timeline
Starting Y-axis above zero to exaggerate changes

visualizations.name: Bar Chart
visualizations.definition: Uses rectangular bars to compare discrete categories or time periods side by side.
visualizations.when_to_use: Comparing values across categories — segments, features, channels, time buckets.
visualizations.example_answer: I'd use a stacked bar chart showing revenue by subscription tier monthly. The chart reveals that Enterprise revenue grew 40% while SMB declined 10% — informs where to focus sales capacity.
common_mistakes: Using 3D bars (distorts perception)
Too many categories (>8) makes bars unreadable
Pie charts instead of bars for comparison

visualizations.name: Heatmap
visualizations.definition: Encodes values as color intensity on a 2D grid — typically time vs. day or feature vs. user segment.
visualizations.when_to_use: Finding patterns across two categorical dimensions simultaneously — time patterns, feature usage density.
typical_pm_use_cases: Feature engagement matrix by user segment
visualizations.example_answer: A 7-day × 24-hour heatmap of sessions shows 80% of activity between Tuesday–Thursday, 9am–6pm. Weekend usage is near zero — this is a pure work tool. Scheduling push notifications on Monday 8am will maximize open rates.
common_mistakes: Using too many color gradients
Not normalizing values across rows/columns making comparison meaningless

visualizations.name: Funnel Chart
visualizations.definition: Visualizes sequential step-by-step drop-off rates through a conversion or user flow.
visualizations.when_to_use: Any time you need to find where users abandon a flow — onboarding, checkout, signup, activation.
visualizations.example_answer: Funnel: Homepage (100%) → Signup (42%) → Onboarding step 1 (38%) → Step 2 (21%) → Activation (14%). The 45% drop from step 1 to step 2 is the critical leak. I'd qualitatively investigate with session replays and run an A/B test on simplifying step 2.
common_mistakes: Not accounting for time lag between steps
Using same-session funnels when users naturally take days between steps

visualizations.name: Cohort Chart
visualizations.definition: Groups users by a shared start event (e.g., signup date) and tracks their behavior over time side by side.
visualizations.when_to_use: Comparing retention or behavior across user groups acquired at different times — isolates trend from mix shift.
visualizations.example_answer: Cohort chart shows January cohort has 28% D30 retention vs March cohort at 18%. The drop correlates with our pricing change in February — new users are less committed. March cohort also churns faster in week 2.
common_mistakes: Not aligning cohorts by relative time (weeks since signup) instead of absolute calendar time — conflates seasonality with behavior

visualizations.name: Scatter Plot
visualizations.definition: Plots two continuous variables as points to reveal correlation, clusters, or outliers.
visualizations.when_to_use: When exploring the relationship between two metrics or identifying user segments with unusual behavior.
visualizations.example_answer: Scatter plot of sessions per week vs D30 retention reveals a clear inflection: users with 4+ sessions/week retain at 70%; below that, it drops to 25%. This defines our engagement activation threshold for the north star metric.
common_mistakes: Inferring causation from correlation
Not labeling outliers that might be data quality issues or distinct segments

statistical_tools.name: Confidence Interval
statistical_tools.definition: A range that, with a stated probability (usually 95%), contains the true population parameter.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: When interpreting A/B test results or metric estimates to communicate certainty to stakeholders.
typical_pm_use_cases: Reporting A/B test lift with uncertainty
Estimating DAU range for investor projections
statistical_tools.example_answer: The new checkout flow shows +8% conversion. The 95% CI is [+3%, +13%] — entirely above zero. We can confidently ship. If the CI included zero, we'd need more data.
common_mistakes: Treating a 95% CI as '95% chance the true value is in this range'
Reporting point estimates without CIs to stakeholders

statistical_tools.name: P-value
statistical_tools.definition: The probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the data if the null hypothesis (no effect) were true.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: When deciding whether an A/B test result is statistically significant and not due to random chance.
typical_pm_use_cases: Determining if a feature launch moved a metric
statistical_tools.example_answer: p=0.03 means there's only a 3% probability this result happened by chance under the null. Below our α=0.05 threshold — we reject the null and call it significant. But always pair with effect size — a p=0.001 result with 0.1% lift isn't worth shipping.
common_mistakes: P-hacking (running test until p<0.05)
Confusing p-value with effect size or practical significance
Using p<0.05 as a sacred threshold

statistical_tools.name: A/B Testing
statistical_tools.definition: A controlled experiment that randomly assigns users to control and treatment groups to measure the causal effect of a change.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: Whenever you need causal evidence that a product change improves a metric before full rollout.
statistical_tools.example_answer: I'd A/B test the new onboarding flow. Primary metric: D7 retention. Guardrail metric: D1 completion rate. Run for 2 weeks, 50/50 split, min 5,000 users per arm for 80% power to detect a 5% lift. Ship if p<0.05 and CI fully above zero.
common_mistakes: Peeking at results before reaching sample size
Testing multiple variants without correcting for multiple comparisons
Ignoring novelty effect

statistical_tools.name: Power Analysis
statistical_tools.definition: Statistical process to determine the probability of correctly detecting a real effect given sample size, significance level, and effect size.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: Before running any A/B test — to determine if you have enough traffic to detect the expected effect.
typical_pm_use_cases: Deciding if you can detect a 3% vs 10% lift given your DAU
statistical_tools.example_answer: With 2,000 daily users per variant, 80% power, α=0.05, and a baseline conversion of 10%, we can detect a minimum detectable effect of ~2.5%. If we only expect 1% lift, we need 3x the traffic or 3x the time — not worth running.
common_mistakes: Running underpowered tests and concluding 'no effect' from null results
Setting unrealistically small MDE to reduce sample size requirements

statistical_tools.name: Sample Size Calculation
statistical_tools.definition: Formula to determine the minimum number of observations needed to detect an effect with specified statistical power and significance.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: At the experiment design phase — before launching any test, to avoid underpowered or wasteful experiments.
typical_pm_use_cases: Determining if a feature has enough usage to be testable
statistical_tools.example_answer: Baseline CVR = 5%, target MDE = 1pp (20% relative lift), α=0.05, power=80%. Each arm needs ~3,800 users. With 500 daily users per arm, that's ~8 days. I'd run for 2 weeks to cover weekly seasonality.
common_mistakes: Ignoring seasonality when calculating runtime from daily traffic
Not accounting for the fact that you need both arms — doubling the total sample needed

statistical_tools.name: Standard Deviation
statistical_tools.definition: Measures how much individual data points deviate from the mean — quantifies spread or variability in a dataset.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: When describing the variability of a metric, detecting anomalies, or comparing consistency across segments.
typical_pm_use_cases: Session length variability by user type
statistical_tools.example_answer: Our DAU averages 100K with σ=5K. Yesterday's 82K is 3.6 standard deviations below mean — statistically anomalous. This isn't noise; something broke. I'd check for data pipeline failures, app crashes, or a major competitor launch.
common_mistakes: Reporting mean without standard deviation — hides whether the mean is meaningful or driven by outliers

statistical_tools.name: Variance
statistical_tools.definition: The square of standard deviation — average of squared differences from the mean; measures dispersion in a dataset.
statistical_tools.when_to_use: In statistical modeling, comparing metric consistency across groups, or understanding signal-to-noise ratio.
typical_pm_use_cases: Comparing engagement metric stability across user segments
Assessing whether a metric is reliable enough to use as a north star
statistical_tools.example_answer: Retention variance is high for new users (σ²=120) but low for power users (σ²=8). The new user segment is too unpredictable to use D7 retention as a reliable experiment metric — I'd use activation rate instead which has lower variance and faster signal.
common_mistakes: Confusing variance with standard deviation in communication — always convert to SD for stakeholder-facing communication

product_analysis_tools.name: Cohort Analysis
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: Are newer users behaving differently than older users, and is product quality improving over time?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Cohort retention grid (heatmap with weeks on X-axis, cohort on Y-axis) or multi-line retention curve.
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Separates product improvement signal from mix shift. If Jan cohort retains at 35% and Jun cohort at 22%, product regression happened — not just seasonality.
product_analysis_tools.example: June cohort has significantly lower D30 retention. It coincides with the new onboarding flow. Either the new flow is worse, or we changed acquisition channels and brought in lower-intent users — segment to disentangle.

product_analysis_tools.name: Funnel Analysis
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: Where exactly are users abandoning a critical flow, and what is the magnitude of loss at each step?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Funnel chart (stepped bar chart showing absolute and % drop-off at each stage).
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Quantifies the revenue/retention impact of each bottleneck, enabling prioritization by expected lift.
product_analysis_tools.example: Of 10K users who start checkout, 4K complete it. The biggest drop (40%) is at payment entry. Fixing payment UX could recover ~$200K/month in revenue assuming average order value.

product_analysis_tools.name: Retention Analysis
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: How many users return after their first session, and at what rate do they form a habit?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Retention curve (line chart: day N on X, % retained on Y) or cohort grid.
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Identifies if the product has achieved product-market fit (flattening curve) or continues to lose all users (curve hits zero). Reveals the 'retention ceiling.'
product_analysis_tools.example: D1=55%, D7=30%, D30=18%, D90=15% — the curve flattens after D30. 15% of users form a durable habit. Focus on moving the D7→D30 slope, not just D1.

product_analysis_tools.name: Segmentation
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: Which user groups behave differently, and which segments drive the most value or churn?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Bar charts comparing metric by segment; scatter plots coloring by segment; distribution histograms.
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Reveals that aggregate metrics hide opposing trends in subgroups. Power users mask new user struggles. Mobile vs web, geography, plan tier — each may tell a different story.
product_analysis_tools.example: Overall DAU flat, but breaking by platform: web DAU down 20%, mobile DAU up 35%. The product is shifting to mobile-first and we're optimizing the wrong surface.

product_analysis_tools.name: Root Cause Analysis
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: What caused a metric to move — was it a product change, data issue, external factor, or user behavior shift?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Time series with event annotations; decomposition charts; segmented line charts to isolate the variable.
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Prevents wrong conclusions and wasted engineering cycles. Forces PMs to separate correlation from causation before acting.
product_analysis_tools.example: DAU dropped 12% on Thursday. Step 1: rule out data pipeline issues. Step 2: check if correlated with a specific deployment. Step 3: segment by platform — iOS DAU dropped 25%, Android flat. Step 4: iOS build pushed Wednesday — likely culprit. Hot-fix first, analyze second.

product_analysis_tools.name: Churn Analysis
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: Who churns, when do they churn, and what behavioral signals predict churn before it happens?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Survival curves; churn by cohort heatmap; feature usage comparison (churned vs retained users).
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Identifies the behavioral leading indicators of churn enabling proactive intervention.
product_analysis_tools.example: Churned users had an average of 1.2 sessions in their last 2 weeks vs 6.4 for retained users. If we flag users below 2 sessions/week and trigger a re-engagement email, we can intervene at-risk users before they cancel.

product_analysis_tools.name: User Journey Mapping
product_analysis_tools.question_it_answers: What is the actual path users take through the product, where do they deviate, and where do they get stuck?
product_analysis_tools.graph_used: Sankey diagram; flow chart; path analysis showing common routes with edge weights.
product_analysis_tools.pm_insight_generated: Reveals unintended high-traffic paths, navigation dead ends, and the gap between designed flows and actual user behavior.
product_analysis_tools.example: 40% of users navigate from Home → Settings → Back to Home without completing any action. This 'dead loop' suggests confusion about the IA. They're looking for something they can't find — time for a card sort and IA audit.

top_20_concepts.insight: Every PM interview question eventually needs one. Know your product's core value delivery metric.
Signals habit formation. Above 0.5 = strong daily habit. Below 0.2 = weak engagement despite large user base.
Flattening curve = PMF. Asymptotic to zero = no PMF. The shape matters more than the absolute number.
Always find the biggest drop as a percentage, multiply by value, and prioritize highest-impact bottleneck.
Hypothesis → Primary metric + guardrails → Sample size → Runtime → Ship decision based on CI, not just p-value.
Minimum 3x for SaaS. Below 1x = unsustainable. Above 5x = under-investing in growth.
Never trust aggregate metrics alone. Cohorts reveal if product quality is improving or mix shift is masking problems.
CIs show magnitude and direction of effect. P-values only show statistical significance — not practical importance.
Always segment before diagnosing. Platform, geography, user tenure, and acquisition channel tell different stories.
Activation predicts long-term retention. It's your fastest leading indicator — D1 actions predict D30 outcomes.
Metric drops need structured investigation: rule out data issues, segment to isolate, correlate with events.
Never optimize a primary metric without defining what you won't sacrifice. Guardrails prevent Goodhart's Law.
User churn hides expansion revenue. Revenue churn (net) is the real health signal — negative NRR is a crisis.
Underpowered tests produce false negatives. Always calculate MDE and required n before running, not after.
A metric 2+ SDs from mean warrants investigation. 3+ SDs = likely real signal, not noise.
When behavior patterns is the question, a day-hour heatmap reveals usage clusters that line charts miss.
Identify behavioral leading indicators of churn — low session frequency, feature abandonment — and intervene proactively.
Sessions/week vs retention scatter plot reveals the engagement threshold that predicts retained vs churned users.
The actual user path in your product is always different from the designed one. Path analysis reveals real behavior.
CAC ÷ Monthly Gross Margin. Under 12 months is healthy for SaaS. Critical for capital efficiency narrative.

if_x_then_y_triggers.interviewer_says: Run an experiment / test a feature
Metric anomaly / sudden spike or drop
Is this result real or noise?
What does user behavior look like?

key_formulas.label: Stickiness
key_formulas.benchmark: Above 0.5 = strong habit. Below 0.2 = weak engagement.

key_formulas.label: LTV
key_formulas.benchmark: Or: ARPU × Gross Margin × Average Customer Lifespan.

key_formulas.label: LTV/CAC Target
key_formulas.benchmark: Minimum 3x for SaaS. Below 1x = unsustainable. Above 5x = under-investing.

key_formulas.label: Payback Period
key_formulas.formula: CAC ÷ Monthly Gross Margin per Customer
key_formulas.benchmark: Under 12 months = healthy SaaS. Over 18 = capital efficiency risk.

key_formulas.label: Confidence Level
key_formulas.benchmark: Industry standard: 95% (α=0.05). CI excludes zero → statistically significant.

key_formulas.label: Statistical Power
key_formulas.benchmark: Standard: 80%. Probability of detecting a real effect when it exists.

retention_benchmarks.pmf_signal: Flattening retention curve = product-market fit achieved

pm_answer_structure.label: Clarify
pm_answer_structure.action: What product? What time window? What metric baseline?

pm_answer_structure.label: Validate
pm_answer_structure.action: Which tool and visualization would confirm or deny each?

pm_answer_structure.label: Recommend
pm_answer_structure.action: Data-backed action with expected impact and how to measure success.

golden_rules: Correlation ≠ Causation. Only A/B tests establish causal effect.
Every A/B test needs 1 primary metric + 2 guardrails. Optimizing one metric shouldn't break another.
Never report aggregate metrics without segmentation. Platform, geography, and tenure tell different stories.
Drop-off priority = biggest drop% × average value. Fix the highest revenue leak first.
Underpowered tests produce false negatives. Always calculate sample size before running.
p<0.05 without effect size is meaningless. A tiny lift with p=0.001 is still not worth shipping.
